_schema: The low-ESR electrolytic across the ESC's input pads — plans/2026-09-10-power-room-design.md §3.4, slice PW1. Two tiers, as in every other catalog file: `specs` is physics-bearing and `catalog` is browsing metadata only. Colour, price and vendor links are banned by name, from either block. THE REASON THIS FILE EXISTS IS THAT THE PART EXISTS. CONTINUE-HERE.md §7 calls the cap 'not optional on 6S, the most commonly forgotten essential part', and the value of modelling it is almost entirely that the app says so; what microfarad it recommends is secondary. So the check that reads this file states a RULE in the guess voice — 'a 6S build wants roughly 470-1000 uF at 35 V' — and does not compute a ripple current. It cannot: sizing a cap properly needs the ESC's switching frequency and the bus inductance of the harness, and NEITHER IS PUBLISHED FOR ANY BOARD IN escs.json, nor will be. A ripple current derived from two numbers nobody published would be a construction wearing a measurement's confidence, which is the one thing design §0 still refuses. 'esr_ohm' is carried, shown, and read by NO check — the same treatment escs.json gives burst_a and connectors.json gives contact_resistance_ohm, and it is named here so that a future ripple model has a field to land in rather than a field to invent. 'capacitance_uf' and 'voltage_v' are what the §3.4 rule compares against; 'diameter_mm' and 'height_mm' are the can's published body dimensions and sit in `specs` for the reason a battery's do — they are read by geometry, since a 12.5 x 20 mm can is a real object that has to go somewhere on a stack and a 6.3 x 11 mm one fits under it. VOLTAGE RATING IS A HARD FLOOR, NOT A PREFERENCE: an electrolytic run above its rated voltage fails, and a 6S pack comes off the charger at 25.2 V, which is why there is no 25 V part in this file above the 1-2S rows. Mass is the whole can including leads. Entries are ordered by capacitance and then voltage, which gives a picker an ascending order without anything sorting it.

parts.name: 100 uF 16 V low-ESR
parts.source: class-typical 6.3 x 11 mm low-ESR aluminium electrolytic, not a specific product. Dimensions follow the standard Panasonic FR / Nichicon HD case size for 100 uF 16 V. ESR and mass are ROUGH: ESR varies by more than a factor of two across series at this size, and mass is under a gram and unpublished.

parts.name: 220 uF 16 V low-ESR
parts.source: class-typical 6.3 x 11 mm low-ESR aluminium electrolytic, not a specific product. This is the small one the 1-2S end of the catalog actually uses — it fits under a whoop AIO where a 35 V can does not. ESR and mass are ROUGH, as above.

parts.name: 220 uF 25 V low-ESR
parts.source: class-typical 8 x 12 mm low-ESR aluminium electrolytic, not a specific product. 25 V is a 4S part and NOT a 6S one: a 6S pack rests at 22.2 V and charges to 25.2 V, which is over this can's rating before the motors have turned. ESR and mass are ROUGH.

parts.name: 330 uF 35 V low-ESR
parts.source: class-typical 10 x 12.5 mm low-ESR aluminium electrolytic, not a specific product. Sits just BELOW the 470-1000 uF the §3.4 rule asks for on 6S, deliberately: the rule has to have something to be unsatisfied by, or a check that never fires is a check that has never been shown to work. ESR and mass are ROUGH.

parts.name: 470 uF 35 V low-ESR
parts.source: class-typical 10 x 16 mm low-ESR aluminium electrolytic, not a specific product. The bottom of the §3.4 rule's band and the most commonly fitted cap on a 6S 5-inch. ESR and mass are ROUGH.

parts.name: 1000 uF 35 V low-ESR
parts.source: class-typical 12.5 x 20 mm low-ESR aluminium electrolytic, not a specific product. The top of the §3.4 rule's band, and a real object: a 12.5 mm can standing 20 mm off the ESC pads is taller than most stacks have room for, which is exactly why the dimensions are in `specs` and not left implicit. ESR and mass are ROUGH.
